note: The Architecture Engineering decision catalogue. Each decision is evaluated by explore.ts: rules in order, the first rule whose named factors are all known and matching fires; a rule blocked only by an unknown factor is reported as missing information; no rule firing means the fallback, which is always the simplest alternative. Pattern ids must resolve in registry.json (checked by patterns:validate). Content is English, like the registry.

decisions.title: Where the computation runs
decisions.question: Which placement should execute this unit of work: the browser main thread, a browser worker, a server request, a background job or a separately deployed service?
decisions.description: Placement is where code executes, separate from the language it is written in and from the unit it is deployed in. The default is the SvelteKit server request: one deployment, one trust zone, the code next to the data. Work moves to the device when the data is already there or must work offline, to a job when it outlives a request, and to a separate service only on an explicit trigger.

problem.workload: One unit of work a feature needs performed — a transformation, a calculation, a query, a conversion.
functional: Produce the result the feature needs
Respect who may see the inputs and outputs
nonfunctional: Cost and operational burden proportional to the need
constraints: Secrets and authorization never execute on the device
Serverless request handlers have a hard duration limit
assumptions: The v10r stack: SvelteKit on a serverless host, Postgres, an optional container host

alternatives.approach: Run it on the browser main thread
drawbacks: Blocks input and rendering while it runs
Bounded by the slowest supported device
prerequisites: The data is already on the device
contraindications: Anything over roughly one frame budget per interaction
alternatives.prefer_when: the data is on the device and the work fits inside an interaction budget (well under 50 ms on a slow phone)

alternatives.approach: Run it in a browser Web Worker
drawbacks: postMessage copies data unless it is transferred
A second module and a message protocol to maintain
prerequisites: Vite worker.format 'es' and CSP worker-src (see workers.md)
contraindications: Tiny tasks where messaging costs more than the work
alternatives.prefer_when: the data is on the device and the work is long enough to block input

alternatives.approach: Run it in the SvelteKit server request handler
benefits: One deployment and one trust zone
Next to the database and the secrets
Easiest to test and to change
drawbacks: Every call pays a network round trip
Bounded by the host's request duration limit
contraindications: Work longer than the host's request limit
Work that must survive the user leaving
alternatives.prefer_when: the work needs secrets, authorization or server data, and finishes well inside a request

alternatives.approach: Run it as a background job or queue worker
technologies: Postgres claimed rows (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
drawbacks: The result arrives later — needs a status and a way to notify
prerequisites: A scheduler (cron on serverless, a persistent process on a container)
contraindications: Results the user waits for interactively
Work small enough for the request
alternatives.prefer_when: the work runs for minutes, must continue without the user, or must retry on failure

alternatives.approach: Run it in a separately deployed compute service
benefits: A different runtime or language where it is genuinely needed
drawbacks: A network hop on every call
A second deployment, credential and contract to maintain
prerequisites: A typed contract and a failure model
contraindications: Speed alone — the boundary is not a speed argument
alternatives.prefer_when: the work needs a different runtime, isolation, or independent scaling — and the team accepts a second deployment

rules.because: Secrets and authorization decisions must never ship to the device; the server request is the simplest placement that keeps them there.
Business rules and authorization are enforced where the client cannot change them: the server, in a framework-free domain.
The work must continue without the user's request, so it cannot live in a request handler or the browser.
Minutes of work exceed serverless request limits and the user's patience; a job with a status is the honest shape.
Offline work can only run on the device, and moderate or heavy CPU belongs off the main thread.
Offline work can only run on the device; light work fits on the main thread.
Heavy server-side compute, a container host and a team that accepts a second deployment are the trigger for a dedicated compute service.
Heavy server-side work nobody waits for is a job: it leaves the request path and gets retries.
The data is already on the device; uploading it costs more than computing it there, and the CPU belongs off the main thread.
The data is on the device and the work is light; a worker would cost more in messaging than it saves.

fallback.because: Nothing in the workload asks for more: the server request is the simplest placement — one deployment, one trust zone, next to the data.

changes_when: The work grows past the host's request duration limit (→ background job)
The data must stay on the device, or offline operation becomes required (→ browser)
A measured hot loop needs a different runtime and the team accepts a second deployment (→ separate service)

evidence.claim: Web Worker offload and the claim-based queue worker both run in v10r with tests.
evidence.limitations: Shows the shapes work; does not measure their overhead on your workload.

evidence.claim: A separate service adds a network hop: about 0.7 ms p50 on loopback, about 67 ms per call hosted (Render Free, Frankfurt), and a cold start that can exceed an 8 s deadline.
evidence.conditions: Loopback and controlled-lab runs on a development machine; hosted rows on Render Free, Frankfurt, 2026-10-23, called from the developer's network.
evidence.limitations: One service, one region, a small payload. Your host, region and payload change the numbers.

evidence.claim: postMessage payloads up to roughly 100 KiB fit a 100 ms interaction budget; transferring an ArrayBuffer is near-constant time.
evidence.limitations: Measured in 2019 browsers; a heuristic, not a constant.

revisit_when: A request handler starts timing out
Users report jank during a computation
A second team or runtime needs to own the work

migrations.path: Keep the domain function; call it from a registered job instead of the request, and return a job id with a status endpoint or SSE update.
migrations.implications: Adds a status lifecycle, idempotency and retries; the UI must handle 'pending'.

migrations.path: Move the pure core into #lib/workers/ and keep the impure shell on the main thread; transfer buffers instead of copying.
migrations.implications: Adds a worker module, CSP worker-src and the Vite worker format setting.

migrations.path: Extract the hot path behind a typed contract (OpenAPI → generated types), call it through one service client with a deadline and a failure kind per cause.
migrations.implications: A second deployment, a credential, a contract to version, and every call can now fail on its own.

decisions.confirmation: Architecture Studio's engineering checks flag CPU-intensive work on the main thread, long-running work in request handlers, and secrets on browser nodes.

decisions.title: Which runtime and language
decisions.question: Which runtime should execute the hot path — TypeScript, SQL inside the database, Rust compiled to WebAssembly in the browser, or native Rust in a service?
decisions.description: Language and runtime are a separate dimension from placement. Rust is not automatically faster than JavaScript, and WebAssembly is not automatically faster than optimised JavaScript: Wasm pays off on compute-dense loops over typed data that stays resident in linear memory, and loses when every call copies data across the boundary. Choose it on measurement, not reputation.

problem.workload: The hot path of a unit of work, once its placement is known.
functional: Produce the same result in whichever runtime is chosen
nonfunctional: Throughput or latency of the hot loop
constraints: The dev container is Rust-free; Wasm is built in an ephemeral container and vendored
assumptions: A parity test can prove two implementations produce identical output

alternatives.approach: TypeScript in the chosen placement
benefits: No build toolchain beyond the app's
Modern JITs are fast for most work
drawbacks: Less predictable performance for tight numeric loops
alternatives.prefer_when: almost always — until a measurement shows the hot loop is the bottleneck

alternatives.approach: SQL executed inside the database
benefits: Filters and aggregates next to the data
Moves only the result over the network
drawbacks: Business logic in SQL is harder to test and to read
Ties the logic to one engine
contraindications: Business rules that need application context
Logic that is clearer and fast enough in TypeScript
alternatives.prefer_when: the work is filtering, joining or aggregating data that already lives in the database

alternatives.approach: Rust compiled to WebAssembly, run in a browser worker
benefits: Predictable throughput on compute-dense loops over typed arrays
No GC in the hot loop
drawbacks: Copying across the JS/Wasm boundary can erase the gain
A Rust toolchain and a vendored artifact to keep fresh
prerequisites: A JS twin and a byte-parity test
alternatives.prefer_when: a measured, compute-dense loop over typed data that can stay resident in Wasm memory

alternatives.approach: Native Rust in a separately deployed service
prerequisites: A reason beyond speed: isolation, existing Rust code, independent scaling
alternatives.prefer_when: heavy server-side compute that justifies its own deployment

rules.because: Filtering and aggregation over database data belong in SQL, next to the data; only the result crosses the network.
A heavy, numeric hot loop over device data is the one case where Wasm in a worker can pay off — confirm it with a parity-gated benchmark before committing.
Heavy backend compute with a container host and high complexity tolerance can justify native Rust in its own service.

fallback.because: No measured hot loop is stated: TypeScript is the default until a benchmark says otherwise.

changes_when: A profile shows a compute-dense loop dominating (→ consider Wasm or native)
Boundary copies dominate the Wasm timing (→ back to TypeScript)
The data moves into the database (→ SQL for filtering and aggregation)

evidence.claim: A Rust blur kernel against its line-for-line JS twin, with copy-in, compute and copy-out timed separately and a deliberately losing per-call-copy case.
evidence.limitations: Runs on the reader's device; nothing is recorded. The docs describe blur at about 2–4× in 2026 engines — one kernel, not a general rule.

evidence.claim: The benchmark protocol: byte-parity-gated identical algorithms, warm-up, counterbalanced rounds, medians, init cost reported.
WebAssembly ran on average 45–55% slower than native code across SPEC benchmarks in Firefox and Chrome.
evidence.limitations: 2019 browsers, compiled C benchmarks; says nothing about Wasm against optimised JavaScript for your workload.

revisit_when: A benchmark on representative data contradicts the current choice
The Wasm artifact's freshness gate starts failing often

migrations.path: Write the Rust kernel as a line-for-line twin, add the parity test, benchmark both with init and copies counted, and keep the JS path as the fallback.
migrations.implications: A vendored artifact, a build container, CSP wasm-unsafe-eval, and a Safari feature floor.

migrations.path: Delete the kernel and keep the JS twin, which the parity test already pins.
migrations.implications: Removes the toolchain; performance returns to the JS baseline you measured.

decisions.confirmation: The wasm pattern's parity test and benchmark protocol; a Studio wasm-module node outside a browser placement is flagged as unsupported.

decisions.title: How the parts communicate
decisions.question: How should the caller and the work talk: an in-process call, HTTP/REST, typed RPC, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, or a database-mediated queue?
decisions.description: Every network boundary adds latency, a failure mode and a contract. Inside the modular monolith a call is a function call. Synchronous request/response fits short work; long work becomes asynchronous with an explicit status; server-to-client push is SSE unless the client must also push at high frequency.

problem.workload: A caller that needs work done, and possibly a result or a stream of updates.
functional: Deliver the request and the result
State what happens when either side fails
constraints: Serverless hosts do not keep WebSocket connections
Every crossing of a trust boundary needs authentication

alternatives.approach: An in-process function call through a domain barrel
benefits: No network, no serialization, no partial failure
contraindications: Caller and callee in different deployment units
alternatives.prefer_when: caller and callee are in the same deployment — which in a modular monolith is most of the time

alternatives.approach: HTTP/REST request and response
drawbacks: Untyped unless a schema is shared
prerequisites: Authentication on every endpoint that crosses a trust boundary
alternatives.prefer_when: an external or browser client calls short, cacheable or resource-shaped operations

alternatives.approach: Typed RPC over HTTP with a generated contract
benefits: Compile-time agreement between caller and service
drawbacks: A contract chain to generate and check
alternatives.prefer_when: the app calls a separately deployed service it owns

alternatives.approach: Server-Sent Events for server-to-client updates
drawbacks: Long-lived connections on serverless are bounded
alternatives.prefer_when: the server pushes progress, notifications or collaboration updates and the client's own writes are ordinary requests

alternatives.approach: WebSockets for bidirectional real-time messages
drawbacks: Reconnection, ordering and backpressure are yours
prerequisites: A container or a managed real-time service
alternatives.prefer_when: many small messages flow both ways with tight latency, on a host that keeps connections

alternatives.approach: Database-mediated queue (outbox rows claimed by a worker)
benefits: Written in the same transaction as the change
alternatives.prefer_when: the work is asynchronous, must not be lost, and Postgres is already there

rules.because: Work that outlives the request is handed over asynchronously and durably; the outbox delivers at least once without a new broker.
Minutes of work cannot hold a request open; enqueue it and report status.
Bidirectional real-time collaboration on a host that keeps connections is what WebSockets are for.
Serverless hosts do not keep WebSockets; push updates with SSE and send edits as ordinary requests.
A dedicated compute service the app owns is called through a typed, generated contract with deadlines.
A lightweight API for external or browser clients is plain HTTP/REST with standard caching and errors.
Uploads are HTTP requests — ideally straight to object storage through a signed URL, with the app recording the result.

fallback.because: Nothing requires a boundary: inside the modular monolith the simplest communication is a function call.

changes_when: The callee moves to another deployment unit (→ HTTP or typed RPC)
The work becomes long or must not be lost (→ queue)
The host starts keeping connections and the client pushes often (→ WebSocket)

evidence.claim: The outbox queue worker: atomic SKIP LOCKED claim, attempts fence, retry with backoff, stale-claim reaper.
evidence.limitations: Reference behaviour; polling latency depends on the drain interval you choose.

evidence.claim: A typed service client with a deadline, bounded body, one failure kind per cause and retry only on idempotent calls.
evidence.limitations: One service; the contract chain is the reusable part.

evidence.claim: One domain serves UI, REST, AI tools and jobs through in-process calls; adapters are thin.
evidence.limitations: Reasoning and gate tests, not a performance measurement.

revisit_when: A synchronous call starts timing out
The host changes between serverless and container

migrations.path: Put the callee behind a contract; keep the domain function as the implementation on the other side.
migrations.implications: Adds latency, partial failure and a version to manage on every call.

migrations.path: Enqueue in the same transaction as the change; return an id; deliver status by SSE or polling.

decisions.confirmation: Studio checks flag protocols a target cannot accept, WebSockets on request-only placements, and network connections with no stated failure handling.

decisions.title: Where the data lives
decisions.question: Where should the authoritative copy of this data live: PostgreSQL, browser memory, IndexedDB, a cache, object storage, or a graph database?
decisions.description: Storage placement is not computation placement. The authoritative copy lives where it can be protected, backed up and queried; caches and device copies are derived from it. Postgres is the default; other stores are added for a reason the default cannot meet.

problem.workload: Data a feature reads and writes.
functional: Keep the data correct and available
Let the right parties read it
constraints: Personal data falls under GDPR retention and export
Large binaries do not belong in table rows

alternatives.approach: PostgreSQL as the authoritative store
drawbacks: A network round trip per query from serverless
contraindications: Data that must never leave the device
alternatives.prefer_when: the data is shared, structured, or must be correct under concurrent writes

alternatives.approach: Browser memory only (state that never leaves the device)
benefits: No upload, no server cost, private by construction
contraindications: Data that must survive the session
alternatives.prefer_when: the data is the user's own working set and does not need to outlive the page

alternatives.approach: IndexedDB on the device, synchronised with the server
drawbacks: Sync and conflict resolution are yours
prerequisites: A sync strategy and a server source of truth
contraindications: Data that must be authoritative on the device
alternatives.prefer_when: offline operation is required

alternatives.approach: A cache in front of the authoritative store
benefits: Protects the database from hot keys
drawbacks: A second store to reason about
contraindications: As the only copy of anything
alternatives.prefer_when: measured repeat reads dominate and slightly stale data is acceptable

alternatives.approach: Object storage for files and large binaries
alternatives.prefer_when: the data is files, media or large blobs

alternatives.approach: A graph database for relationship-first queries
drawbacks: A second database to keep fresh
prerequisites: A traversal-heavy query that Postgres recursive CTEs serve poorly
alternatives.prefer_when: the queries are traversals over many-hop relationships

rules.because: Offline operation needs a durable copy on the device, synchronised with a server source of truth.
Files and media belong in object storage; the database keeps their metadata.
The data starts on the device and nothing needs it elsewhere; keeping it in memory avoids an upload and a privacy surface.
Large uploads go straight to object storage through a signed URL rather than through the app.

fallback.because: Postgres is the default authoritative store: transactions, constraints, one backup and retention story.

changes_when: Offline becomes required (→ IndexedDB plus sync)
Repeat reads are measured as the bottleneck (→ add a cache)
Queries become many-hop traversals (→ consider a graph projection)

evidence.claim: Relational and graph patterns, polyglot freshness between Postgres and Neo4j.
evidence.limitations: Shows both work in v10r; no comparative benchmark.

evidence.claim: One database per stack; managed services hold state, never logic.
evidence.limitations: A project principle, not a measurement.

revisit_when: Database read latency dominates a measured trace
Storage cost of blobs in rows grows

migrations.path: Keep Postgres authoritative; add a read-through cache with SWR and singleflight for the measured hot keys only.
migrations.implications: Staleness windows and invalidation become part of the contract.

migrations.path: Persist the working set locally and add a sync path to a server store.
migrations.implications: Conflict resolution and storage eviction handling.

decisions.title: Where data is filtered and aggregated
decisions.question: Should filtering and aggregation run inside the database, in the application server, or in the browser?
decisions.description: Moving computation to the data beats moving data to the computation when the data is large and the result is small. That argues for SQL-side filtering and aggregation — not for business rules inside the database. Application-side processing stays the default for small sets, where TypeScript is clearer and fast enough.

problem.workload: Reading many rows to produce fewer — a filter, a group-by, a top-N, a sum.
functional: Return the correct subset or aggregate
constraints: Serverless functions pay a round trip per query

alternatives.approach: Filter and aggregate in SQL
benefits: Only the result crosses the network
drawbacks: Complex logic in SQL is harder to test and review
prerequisites: An index that supports the query
contraindications: Business rules that need application context
Logic that changes often and is clearer in TypeScript
alternatives.prefer_when: the input is large and the result is small

alternatives.approach: Fetch the rows and process them in TypeScript on the server
benefits: Easy to combine with non-database data
alternatives.prefer_when: the input is small, or the logic needs context the database does not have

alternatives.approach: Process on the device
drawbacks: The data must be on the device first
prerequisites: The data is already on the device, or small enough to send once
contraindications: Data the user may not see in full
alternatives.prefer_when: the data originates on the device or is small, public and re-filtered interactively

rules.because: Querying and aggregating database data: let the database filter and aggregate so only the result crosses the network.
Medium or large inputs in the database are reduced there; transferring them to the app to discard most of them wastes bytes and memory.
The data is already on the device; processing it there avoids an upload.

fallback.because: Small inputs: TypeScript on the server is clearer and fast enough, and keeps logic out of the database.

changes_when: Input sizes grow while results stay small (→ SQL)
The logic gains application context the database lacks (→ application)

evidence.claim: Query budgets pin the number of database round trips per operation and fail the gate when a change adds one.
evidence.limitations: Counts round trips; does not compare SQL-side and app-side processing time or bytes.

evidence.claim: SQL-side reduction is preferable when the input is large and the result small.
evidence.limitations: v10r has no measured app-vs-database comparison yet. This recommendation rests on reasoning, not a recorded measurement.

revisit_when: A trace shows large result sets transferred and then filtered
A query becomes too complex to review

migrations.path: Push the filter or aggregate into the query; add the supporting index; keep a test asserting both give the same result.
migrations.implications: Logic moves into SQL — keep it to filtering and aggregation, not business rules.

decisions.title: What is deployed together
decisions.question: Should this ship as a modular monolith, a monolith on a persistent host, a monolith plus a worker, a monolith plus a compute service, or a distributed system?
decisions.description: Start with a modular monolith whose module boundaries are enforced by gates; split a deployment unit off only on an explicit trigger — a different runtime, isolation, a persistent connection, or independent scaling. Every added unit adds deployment, monitoring, credentials and failure modes.

functional: Run every workload somewhere it fits
assumptions: Vercel for the app; Render or Podman for containers

alternatives.approach: One serverless SvelteKit deployment with enforced module boundaries
benefits: One deployment, one pipeline, one log
Boundaries enforced by tests, so a later split is cheap
contraindications: Work longer than the host's limits without a job runner
alternatives.prefer_when: nothing in the workloads demands a persistent process or a different runtime

alternatives.approach: The same monolith on a persistent container host
alternatives.prefer_when: the app needs persistent connections or in-process background loops

alternatives.approach: The monolith plus a background worker process
technologies: A worker on a container, or scheduled drains on serverless
benefits: Long work leaves the request path
drawbacks: A second process to deploy and watch
prerequisites: A container host, or cron on the serverless host
contraindications: No work that outlives a request
alternatives.prefer_when: work must run in the background continuously

alternatives.approach: The monolith plus a separately deployed compute service
benefits: A different runtime and isolated resources for the heavy part
drawbacks: A second deployment, credential and contract
alternatives.prefer_when: one workload needs its own runtime or scaling and the team accepts the operational cost

alternatives.approach: Several independently deployed services
benefits: Independent deployment and scaling per team
contraindications: A solo developer or a small team
Boundaries not yet proven in a monolith
alternatives.prefer_when: several teams need independent release cycles over boundaries already proven in a modular monolith

rules.because: Heavy backend compute with a container host and high tolerance is the trigger for one extra unit — not for a distributed system.
Real-time connections need a process that stays up; run the same monolith on a persistent host.
Continuous background work on a container host gets its own worker process draining the outbox.

fallback.because: No trigger for a second unit: one serverless deployment with enforced module boundaries is the simplest suitable shape. Background work on serverless runs as scheduled jobs inside it.

changes_when: A workload needs a persistent connection (→ persistent host)
Background work becomes continuous (→ worker)
One workload needs its own runtime or scaling (→ one service)

evidence.claim: Vendor-agnostic scheduling: the registry owns the job, the platform owns the schedule — cron on Vercel, setInterval on a container.
evidence.limitations: Reasoning plus a working registry; no cost comparison.

evidence.claim: A free-tier container service can take longer than an 8 s deadline to wake from cold.
evidence.limitations: One host and plan; paid plans do not sleep.

evidence.claim: Successful service architectures usually started as monoliths; early boundaries are hard to get right.
evidence.limitations: Experience report, not a controlled study.

revisit_when: A workload hits the host's limits
A second team needs independent releases
Operational cost of extra units outweighs their benefit

migrations.path: Move the job registry's drain into a persistent worker; keep cron as the fallback trigger.
migrations.implications: A second process; the outbox and job code are unchanged.

migrations.path: Extract one domain behind a typed contract; deploy it as a container; call it through a service client.
migrations.implications: Network failure handling, a credential and a contract version.

migrations.path: Fold the service back into a domain when its trigger disappears.
migrations.implications: Removes a deployment; the contract tests become unit tests.

decisions.confirmation: Studio comparison counts deployment units and operational requirements, so a variant's added units are visible.

decisions.title: Making slow work fast
decisions.question: When a computation is too slow, what should change first: the algorithm, the thread it runs on, the runtime, the machine, or whether it runs at all?
decisions.description: Most slowness is algorithmic or I/O. Measure first, then change the cheapest thing that the measurement implicates: a better algorithm, moving the work off the main thread, caching a repeated result, and only then a different runtime or machine. Every step adds complexity; none is automatically an improvement.

problem.workload: A unit of work that is, or is expected to be, too slow.
functional: Same result, sooner — or without blocking
constraints: No theoretical score may stand in for a measurement
assumptions: A profile or benchmark can be taken on representative data

alternatives.approach: Measure, then fix the algorithm and data structures in place
drawbacks: Needs a profile to aim at
alternatives.prefer_when: always first

alternatives.approach: Move the work into a Web Worker
benefits: Input stays responsive even if total time is unchanged
drawbacks: Does not make the work itself faster
prerequisites: The work does not need the DOM
contraindications: Work shorter than the messaging cost
alternatives.prefer_when: the problem is jank during interaction, not total duration

alternatives.approach: Port the measured hot loop to Rust/Wasm, inside a worker
benefits: Can speed up compute-dense loops over typed data
prerequisites: A benchmark against an optimised JS twin, with init and copies counted
contraindications: The loop is not the bottleneck
alternatives.prefer_when: a parity-gated benchmark on representative data shows the gain survives init and copies

alternatives.approach: Cache the result of repeated work
benefits: Repeat requests skip the work entirely
contraindications: Personal data in a shared cache
alternatives.prefer_when: measured repeat requests with identical inputs dominate

alternatives.approach: Offload the work from the device to the server
prerequisites: The data may leave the device
contraindications: Large device data with a small result computed once
alternatives.prefer_when: the device is too weak and the data is small or already on the server

rules.because: A heavy numeric loop over a sizeable device-side buffer is the profile where Wasm in a worker can pay off — benchmark it against an optimised JS twin first.
Interactive latency with moderate or heavy device-side work: the first fix is not blocking input.
A lightweight API with interactive latency usually wins most from caching identical repeat requests — after measuring that they repeat.

fallback.because: Measure first: most slowness is algorithmic or I/O, and fixing it in place adds no moving parts.

changes_when: A profile implicates the runtime rather than the algorithm (→ Wasm or native)
The problem is blocking, not duration (→ worker)
Inputs repeat (→ cache)

evidence.claim: Compute, copy-in and copy-out timed separately; the per-call-copy case shows the boundary erasing the gain.
evidence.limitations: Your device, one kernel; nothing recorded.

evidence.claim: Bundle and route weight are ratcheted; initial loading cost of an added runtime is visible in validate:build.
Worker messaging cost scales with payload; transfer avoids the copy.

revisit_when: The performance budget or ratchet regresses
A new profile moves the bottleneck

migrations.path: Inside the existing worker, swap the JS core for a Wasm kernel behind the same message protocol; keep the JS twin and the parity test.
migrations.implications: Adds the wasm artifact and its init cost to the worker's first run.
